description: Parallax brings together curious builders passionate about AI, space, science, and design. We turn NASA data into creative, meaningful solutions through technology and collaboration. We’re looking for teammates in AI/ML, astronomy, Earth observation, software, data visualization, UI/UX, research, and storytelling—especially those who love to build, learn, and explore.
summary: Still Here is a pixel-art interactive science story for ages 10–14 about the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector, a piece of NASA equipment left on the Moon in 1969 that scientists still use today. It answers one question: how can hardware abandoned decades ago keep doing science with no electrical power? Visitors inspect real NASA photos, sort which parts of a laser-ranging system need power (all are on Earth), steer light into a corner-cube mirror, time a laser pulse's round trip and learn why distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2, then step from a single echo to decades of calibrated evidence. Every fact links to a NASA source, and illustrations, practice numbers and the mascot's imagined voice are clearly labelled. It works offline, by keyboard, with reduced motion and on phones, turning a forgotten artifact into reasoning children do themselves.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Still Here follows the Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retro-Reflector through seven short chapters, styled as a retro pixel desktop where each chapter is a window:

1. Two neighbours – a real 1969 photo compares the solar-powered seismometer (silent since August 1969) with the unpowered reflector. Visitors sort the laser, telescope, detector, clock and corner cubes into "on the Moon" or "on Earth" and discover that every powered part is on Earth.

2. The trick – steer a beam into a corner reflector and a flat mirror to see why shaped glass sends light home without anyone aiming it.

3. The round trip – fire a pulse (schematic, not to scale) and learn why one-way distance = speed of light × time ÷ 2, with a visible note on what real ranging must add (atmosphere, motion, calibration).

4. From echo to evidence – detect, calibrate, check and combine, repeat for decades, interpret. One return is never presented as a discovery.

5. Three applied questions with explanatory feedback.

6. Ending – the hardware, the people who keep the measurement running (e.g. Apache Point Observatory), and the knowledge produced, plus a "Mission files" folder that opens the key NASA sources.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It turns a dense topic into reasoning children do themselves, while keeping scientific limits visible. Every claim is traceable to NASA sources through a built-in Sources panel and a public claim ledger in the repository. It shows that "discarded" equipment can keep contributing to science when people on Earth keep measuring.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript built with Vite, with no runtime network dependencies (works offline). Tested with Playwright: 277 automated browser checks at desktop, tablet and mobile sizes, with reduced motion, offline, keyboard-only and without JavaScript, plus unit tests for the physics. Hosted on GitHub Pages; code at https://github.com/pavithrabinu5/still-here (Apache-2.0).

CREATIVITY

A reflector mascot that reacts to answers, walking pixel characters, a title screen with a laser pulse travelling Earth–Moon–Earth, and five discovery stars earned only at real learning milestones.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific accuracy (claims checked against NASA sources; illustrative numbers labelled; no inference of discoveries from one pulse), accessibility (keyboard, contrast, reduced motion, mobile), and clearly separating documented history from imagined narration.
